questions.prompt: What is the difference between an argument label and a parameter name in Swift?

options.text: Argument labels are used in tests, while parameter names are for app code.
options.explanation: Argument labels and parameter names are language rules used in all Swift code.

options.text: Parameter names set data types, while argument labels set default values.
options.explanation: Types and defaults are written after colons and equals signs.

options.text: Argument labels are used when calling; parameter names are used inside the body.
options.explanation: Right. Labels make calls easy to read; parameter names are used inside the body.

options.text: Argument labels only apply to inout parameters; parameter names apply to constants.
options.explanation: Any parameter can have both an argument label and a parameter name.

questions.prompt: Which symbol is used before a parameter name to omit its argument label when calling?

options.text: An underscore `_`, showing no label is needed when calling.
options.explanation: Right. Writing _ before the parameter name removes the argument label.

options.text: An asterisk `*`, marking a pointer to the argument.
options.explanation: Swift does not use asterisks to omit argument labels.

options.text: A question mark `?`, marking the parameter as optional.
options.explanation: Question marks mark optional types, not omitted argument labels.

options.text: A tilde `~`, showing that the parameter has any type.
options.explanation: Swift checks exact types and does not use tilde for parameters.

questions.prompt: Why can you not reassign or change a normal function parameter inside its body?

options.text: Parameters share memory directly with the caller by default.
options.explanation: Normal parameters are passed as constants; inout is used to update caller variables.

options.text: Parameters in Swift are constant `let` values by default.
options.explanation: Right. Swift treats normal function parameters as let constants.

options.text: Parameters automatically become static properties on a type.
options.explanation: Parameters are local to the function call, not static properties.

options.text: Swift functions cannot create any mutable variables inside their body.
options.explanation: Functions can declare local var variables and inout parameters.

questions.prompt: What must you do when calling a function that has an `inout` parameter in Swift?

options.explanation: Only mutable variables declared with var can be passed to inout.

options.text: Put the argument inside double parentheses when calling.
options.explanation: Double parentheses do not pass an inout variable.

options.text: Write the mutating keyword before the function name.
options.explanation: The mutating keyword is for struct methods, not function calls.

options.text: Put an ampersand `&` before the mutable variable name.
options.explanation: Right. The & symbol shows that the variable can change.

options.text: Making the variable a global constant during the call.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an argument label and a parameter name in Swift? Why does Swift use both? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that argument labels are used when calling the function
Explains that parameter names are used inside the function body
Mentions that this makes function calls read like clear English sentences

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, the argument label is used when calling a function. The parameter name is used inside the function body to read the value. Swift uses both so function calls read like clear English sentences. At the same time, the function body keeps short, clear variable names.

questions.prompt: Why are function parameters in Swift `let` constants by default? What happens if you try to change a parameter inside its body, and how can you change a value instead? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that parameters are let constants to stop accidental changes
States that changing a parameter inside the body causes a compile error
Mentions making a local var copy or using inout to change a value

questions.modelAnswer: Function parameters in Swift are `let` constants by default so you do not change input values by mistake. Trying to reassign a parameter inside the body causes a compile error. To change a value, make a local `var` copy inside the function or mark the parameter with `inout`.

questions.prompt: How does an `inout` parameter work in Swift? Explain copy-in copy-out and what symbol is needed when calling. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that inout lets a function change a caller's variable
Explains copy-in copy-out (copied in on entry, changed, copied back on return)
States that callers must pass a var variable with an ampersand &

questions.modelAnswer: An `inout` parameter lets a function change a variable passed by the caller. Swift uses copy-in copy-out: the value is copied in when the function starts, changed, and copied back out when it returns. Callers must pass a mutable `var` variable with `&` before its name.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that functions are first-class citizens in Swift? Give an example of a function type and explain what a higher-order function is. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that functions are values that can be stored in variables, passed, and returned
Gives a valid example of a function type such as (Int, Int) -> Int
Mentions higher-order functions that take or return other functions

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, functions are first-class citizens, so they have types and act like other values. You can store functions in variables, pass them into higher-order functions, or return them from other functions. For example, a function that takes two `Int` values and returns an `Int` has type `(Int, Int) -> Int`.

questions.prompt: Explain implicit returns in Swift functions. When can you omit the `return` keyword? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that single-expression functions can omit the return keyword
States that Swift returns the value of that single expression automatically
Notes that multi-statement functions still require the return keyword

questions.modelAnswer: An implicit return lets a function omit `return` when its whole body is one expression. Swift returns the value of that single expression automatically. If a function has two or more statements, such as local variables or loops, you still must write `return`.
